terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase. In Latin corium is a person’s skin “only in comic or contemptuous sense” (Lewis & Short); this phrase is not in Lewis & Short or the loci collections.

terms.gloss: play with one’s own skin: risk one’s own hide
evidence: Mart. 3.16.4: coriō suō lūdere, at one’s own expense (Lewis & Short s.v. corium)
Apul. M. 7: dē aliēnō coriō lūdere, at another’s expense (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Tull. 54: petere corium, to flog (Lewis & Short s.v. corium)
Traupman 100: corium alicūjus petere, be after someone’s hide
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives it as “to flog”; Traupman uses it for “be after someone’s hide”.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 100, 328, checked against the searchable text and the page image.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
